--- title: "A Short Local Agentic LLM Experiment" subtitle: "Revising a Quarto notebook with machine learning classifier examples" author: "Ben Stockton" date: 2026-07-07 editor: source format: html: code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" code-tools: true code-overflow: wrap number-depth: 3 toc: true toc-location: left toc-expand: 2 toc-depth: 3 link-external-newwindow: true citations-hover: true df-print: paged bibliography: heart.bib draft: true cache: true categories: [local-ai, llm, machine-learning] --- ::: {.callout-warning title="TLDR" icon=true} Local models are no where near ready for anything beyond lossily summarizing text. They certainly aren't ready for use as agentic models for data science-y tasks even as simple as finding and replacing variable names or adding comments throughout a Quarto document. ::: I've been playing around with local language models to figure out if they might be useful at any non-critical part of my workflow. My decision to test local models is primarily motivated by 1) wanting to keep data as local as possible, and 2) not wanting to spend significant money on a tool that might not be useful since I've heard the free and first paid-tier of the flagship models burn through token limits very quickly. Of course, doing this locally severely limits what I can expect and try to do with the models in a reasonable amount of time. In the rest of the post I will go over my local LLM set-up, the test I performed, and some concluding thoughts. The chat log is in a folded code block at the end of this post. ## Local LLM Set-up I am performing these tests on an M2 MacBook Air with 24 GB of RAM and the 8-core CPU/10-core GPU M2 variant. This is a really underpowered set-up for local LLM work, but is what I have for work and seems like a fair a baseline for what specs most data scientists would have access to. The better specs, the better models you can run. I set up LM Studio by directly installing from their [website](https://lmstudio.ai). I followed their [documentation](https://lmstudio.ai/docs/app) to do some minimal set-up and then went over to the [Positron editor](https://positron.posit.co) blog/documentation to configure the [Posit Assistant](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/downloads/positron/) to use local models launched in a local server by LM Studio. I found this process to be fairly straightforward after finding the right documentation online.[^1] [^1]: The only thing to note is that setting up the Custom Model Provider in Posit Assistant requires using port 1337, an OpenAI style API key, and signing in with key in Positron. Setting up the server with a key takes some fiddling, and the key should be stored in a password manager or keyring in case you need it later. Based on this [post](https://simonpcouch.com/blog/2026-04-16-local-agents-2/) by Simon P. Couch, I decided to try out the Gemma 4 models with quantization to cut down the memory footprint to use the largest model possible (`gemma-4-12b-qat`). Anything larger (`gemma-4-26b-a4b-qat` or `gemma-4-31b`), and the model runs so slowly as to be unusable or crashes. Anything smaller (`gemma-4-e4b-qat`), and the model can't figure out how to use the skills provided by the Posit Assistant harness. I'll refer to `gemma-4-12b-qat` and `gemma-4-e4b-qat` as the 12B and 4B models/agents for the rest of the post. ## The Data Science Test Recently, I helped TA for a Machine Learning and AI Bootcamp held internally at NYU School of Medicine. We introduced the students to classification with some basic tree-based models using the `Heart` data set in Chapter 8 of [ISLR2](https://www.statlearning.com/resources-second-edition) and hosted by the [UC Irvine ML Repository](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/45/heart+disease). In this data set, the typical task is to predict whether a patient has heart disease given set of demographics and diagnostic test results. The data were collected for this exact purpose by a team at Cleveland Clinic in the late 1990s/early 2000s [@detranoInternationalApplicationNew1989; @andrasjanosiHeartDisease1989]. The UCI repository shows that the baseline logistic regression accuracy for this task with this data is around 81% which is matched by XGBoost. Our goal wasn't to beat these scores, only to introduce the students to the methods and hyperparameter tuning procedures. The original Quarto notebook can be found [here](_heart_class.qmd). In the bootcamp, we demonstrated decision trees and random forest. In my extended example, I added in XGBoost and BART, but made a few changes from what we sent students. - I switched from using package specific workflows for data pre-processing, model fitting, hyperparameter tuning, and prediction to only using `tidymodels` as a front-end for all of these tasks to simplify code between the models. This was a side test to see if I'd want to use `tidymodels` for instruction in the future as well. - I cut out a lot of the explanatory text outside of the code cells. - I removed a lot of the comments. My goal for the local agent test was to have it: 1. Switch some variable names to more consistent naming conventions like `*_recipe`, `*_spec`, and `*_pred`. 2. Add comments to the R code chunks throughout the notebook. The test started with the 12B agent in planning mode. I wrote a short [README.md file](README.md):
README ```{.md filename="README.md"} # Overview I am helping prepare example analysis code for a course next week. We are going to be reviewing regularization and classification using tree-based methods like Decision Tree, Random Forest, BART, and XGBoost from a statistical perspective for beginners. There are some example slides and notes in the project directory. Can you help me write clean up some examples for classification using the HEART data I have in the `Heart.csv` file? Do not read the file. See `heart_class.qmd` for an example of the first five rows of data. ## Goal Our goal is to classify the outcome `AHD` using the other predictors. 1. Use Decision Trees 2. Use Random Forest 3. Use BART 4. Use XGBoost 4. Provide scaffolding, but leave regularized logistic regression as an exercise for students. ## Constraints We must use R for our analysis. See the other *.qmd files for the allowable packages. Include a list of the allowable packages in your plan. Models should be implemented using `tidymodels`, graphics should be done with `ggplot2` when possible, and data manipulations should be done with `dplyr`, `purrr`, and `tidyr`. ## Course Slides Slides were prepared using Quarto and are saved as *.qmd files. These should serve as reference materials for modeling. Lab session notes are saved as *.Rmd files. These can be used to help write code, but should not serve as references for modeling. ```
I then prompted the 12B agent to write a plan for how to make the edits to the file. It proceeded to write [plan.md](plan.md):
Plan ```{.md filename="plan.md"} # Plan: Refactor `heart_class.qmd` for Beginners ## Goal Refactor `heart_class.qmd` to improve variable consistency, add descriptive comments, and simplify the code for beginner data scientists while preserving the original educational content and model results. ## Proposed Changes ### 1. File Preparation - Create a duplicate file `heart_class_agent.qmd` to avoid modifying the original source. ### 2. Library and Data Setup - **Variable Consistency**: Rename the primary dataset from `heart` to `heart_data` to be more descriptive. - **Comments**: Add clear headers for each section (Data Loading, Preprocessing, Model Training, Evaluation). - **Code Simplification**: - Use `tidymodels` consistent naming (e.g., `heart_rec` to `heart_recipe`). - Standardize the way predictors and outcomes are referenced. ### 3. Model Training & Evaluation Refactoring - **Decision Trees**: - Rename `DT_spec` to `dt_spec`, `DT_wf` to `dt_workflow`, `DT_res` to `dt_results`. - Add comments explaining why `tune()` is used for hyperparameters. - **Random Forest**: - Rename `RF_spec` to `rf_spec`, `RF_wf` to `rf_workflow`, `RF_res` to `rf_results`. - **BART**: - Rename `BART_spec` to `bart_spec`, `BART_wf` to `bart_workflow`, `BART_res` to `bart_results`. - **XGBoost**: - Rename `xgb_spec` to `xgb_spec` (keep, but check consistency), `xgb_wf` to `xgb_workflow`, `xgb_res` to `xgb_results`. ### 4. Visualization and Summary Table - **Consistency**: Ensure all `pred_df` columns are named consistently across the different model blocks. - **Simplification**: - Simplify the `pred_df` construction to reduce complexity for beginners (perhaps use a helper function or more readable `bind_rows`). - Standardize the `ggplot2` themes and labels for consistency. ### 5. Review and Finalization - Verify that all code blocks still produce the same results. - Ensure the narrative flow of the bootcamp is maintained. ## Implementation Steps 1. Copy `heart_class.qmd` to `heart_class_agent.qmd`. 2. Update the `Set-up` section (Libraries and Data Loading). 3. Update the `Train-test Split` and `Recipe` sections. 4. Refactor the Decision Tree section (Naming and Comments). 5. Refactor the Random Forest section (Naming and Comments). 6. Refactor the BART section (Naming and Comments). 7. Refactor the XGBoost section (Naming and Comments). 8. Update the Model Comparison and Visualization sections. 9. Final review of the `.qmd` file. ```
Up to this point, the 12B agent was performing tasks as I would hope it would. The plan is correct and coherent. I asked the 12B agent to complete the first step in its plan file, and after *two* attempts it managed to create a copy of the Quarto file using the `cp` command. I tried this same step with the 4B model and it tried to write a new blank file with the correct file name. After this step, every interaction was tedious and error-filled even with the 12B model. I didn't make it to adding comments to the code after five hours coaxing the model into making the correct variable name replacements. In fact I only managed to partially replace `heart` with `heart_data` in Section 1 of the notebook. Here's the [final Quarto notebook](_heart_class_agent.qmd). The Posit Assistant with the 12B model often gets stuck in a loop of being unable to find the string it wants to edit in the Quarto file and is unable to parse the error message to figure out it is looking for a truncated string rather than the full string. ::: {.callout-important title="Agent Error"} String not found in file: heart_class_agent.qmd. ::: The only positive of this is at least the 12B agent is trying to use the edit tool. With the 4B model, the agent outputs strings like "I will edit the file." without any attempt to use the edit the file. When I try to use the larger mixture of experts model `gemma-4-26b-a4b-qat`, the model is simply too large for the MacBook to run resulting in crashes after only very short string outputs. I couldn't get it to use tools before crashing. ## Concluding Thoughts This experiment was definitely not successful and as a culmination of weeks of tinkering with local LLMs, I just don't think the models that can run on a MacBook Air are ready for even basic coding work to supplement a modern editor like Positron or VS Code. The local models with an agentic harness are like the laziest, slowest, and most incompetent coding assistant you could ask for. They can't even reliably do find-replace. My attempts to use these same local models as reasoning models in a chat interface were better. They can sometimes accurately summarize documents or help draw connections between different concepts or techniques. Occasionally they can help write (low-quality and error-prone) R code if it comes from common R examples. Stan code is lower quality from what I've seen in my testing. Even in the chat interface, the context window gets eaten up quickly despite system prompts encouraging clear and concise answers because the model generates rambling output within the thinking block and within the final output. Often I see the thinking block proceed through an entire chain of thought ending with "But this answer should be clear and concise," but the output will be 1000 words going on and on about the prompted topic. Other times in chats, it will produce an entirely superfluous chain of thought on the wrong modeling approach, e.g. talking about using `lme4` and `glmer` in response to "Help me write a Bayesian logistic regression mixed model". I think there is clearly the beginning of something useful here. There seems to be at least two necessary criteria for local models to take off: accurate responses and reasonably quick processing/response times. The chat interface is closer to being useful. Responses are quick, but often overly superficial, misleading, or misunderstanding. They remind me of how early ChatGPT and Gemini behaved in 2023 or 2024. It's remarkable that I can run models of that quality on a MacBook Air. But it's just a tech demo for now. I wouldn't trust it with anything beyond generating a markdown or LaTeX template. Local agents are not as close, but seem like they'd be even more useful because their tools can help put guardrails against the inaccuracies and hallucinations that take chat sessions off track. I would barely even call their current state on a MacBook Air a tech demo though. They're extremely slow and cannot perform even the most simple text manipulation tasks. The current state of the art for local models on a MacBook Pro or other personal computer with more RAM and a better GPU may be closer to the experience of using frontier remote models. I haven't yet seen enough evidence of that to spend the money to get a better computer for local models or to get the Pro subscriptions to test remote ones. ---
